passage:
Sunday: Dhruv, nine, refused to open the new chess puzzle book. "I'll just get them wrong." His father, Yash, said, "You found a clever trap in yesterday's game. Want to try one puzzle, just to see?"
Wednesday: Dhruv lost three games in a row to his cousin. Yash didn't mention the losses. "I saw you slow down and check each move before touching the piece. That's a strategy." Dhruv shrugged, but he set the board up again.
The next Saturday: At the colony chess club, Dhruv picked the hardest puzzle on the board. He got it wrong twice. "Third try," he muttered, grinning. When a younger boy cried after losing, Dhruv gave him half his biscuit. Yash noticed that too. "That was kind."

qa.q: What did Dhruv give the younger boy?
qa.a: He gave him half his biscuit.

qa.q: What was Dhruv afraid of on Sunday?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting the puzzles wrong, so he didn't want to try.

qa.q: Which kind of praise did Yash choose, and why did it help?
qa.a: He praised Dhruv's strategy of checking moves and later his kindness, not wins, so Dhruv felt safe to try hard puzzles.

qa.q: How might the younger boy at the chess club see Dhruv?
qa.a: He may see Dhruv as kind and friendly, someone who makes losing feel less lonely.

grounding: Over a week, a father praises his son's strategy and kindness rather than results, and the boy starts risking hard puzzles.

passage: Listen, beta. When I, Amandeep, was headmistress at the Ludhiana school, we had a boy called Siddharth, ten, who hid his drawings because his first one had been laughed at. His class teacher, Mrs Bajwa, never said "beautiful" or "talented". She would say, "You tried three shades of green for that tree. Why?" Or, "You helped Rinku with his colours. That was generous." Slowly he stopped hiding his sheets. The next year he entered the district painting contest. He didn't win anything. He came to my office anyway, beaming, and said, "Ma'am, I tried water colours for the first time!" That boy teaches art now, in Amritsar.

qa.q: What did Siddharth try for the first time at the district contest?
qa.a: He tried water colours for the first time.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after the contest, even without a prize, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy; he came to the office beaming to share what he had tried.

qa.q: What choice did Mrs Bajwa make in her praise, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked about his colour choices and praised his generosity instead of calling him talented, so he learned that trying mattered more than results.

qa.q: How might Rinku have felt when Siddharth helped with his colours?
qa.a: He probably felt supported and grateful, and less alone in class.

grounding: A retired headmistress recalls a teacher praising a boy's effort, choices and kindness, which let him risk trying and enjoy it without winning.

passage: The power went out at eight, two hours before Joseph's science model had to be finished, and the little wind turbine still wouldn't spin. By candlelight he tried a smaller blade, then bent the wire, then taped on cardboard fins, muttering. Shalini held the torch. At half past nine the blades gave one slow turn. "It barely moves," Joseph said, face falling. "The winners will have motors." Shalini set the torch down. "I watched you try four different blades in the dark without giving up. When one failed, you changed the angle instead of starting over. That's how engineers think." Joseph looked at the turbine again. "Next year I'll try a gear," he said, already sketching.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: How was Joseph feeling when the blades gave one slow turn?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, comparing it to winners with motors.

qa.q: What kind of praise did Shalini give, and why does it help?
qa.a: She praised his persistence and strategy, not the result, which shows him his worth isn't about winning.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to watch Joseph start sketching a gear?
qa.a: Shalini is probably pleased and relieved, seeing that her praise for his effort made him want to try something harder.

grounding: Shows a parent praising effort and strategy rather than results, so the child feels safe to try hard things.

passage: Neelam walked off the stage of the school hall in Lucknow with her cheeks burning. She had spelled "rhythm" with one h and gone out in the third round. Jyoti-ma'am found her behind the curtain, pulling at her sleeve. "I got out so early. I'm hopeless at spelling." Jyoti-ma'am crouched down. "I saw you practise with flashcards every lunch for two weeks. And when Farhan froze on stage, you whispered 'breathe' to him. That was kind." Neelam sniffed. "But I didn't win." "You tried something hard in front of three hundred people. Want to learn the tricky words with me for next year?" Neelam, after a moment, nodded.

qa.q: Which word did Neelam misspell?
qa.a: "rhythm", with one h.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling behind the curtain?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hopeless after going out early.

qa.q: What did Jyoti-ma'am praise, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Her practice, her kindness to Farhan and her courage, which shows her worth isn't only about winning.

qa.q: If you were Farhan, how might you feel about Neelam's whisper?
qa.a: Grateful and less alone, since someone helped in a scary moment.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher praising effort and kindness after a loss, helping a child risk trying again.

passage:
"I lost all five games, Ammi. All five."
Parveen handed him a glass of water. "You played five full games against bigger kids. How did it feel to keep going?"
"Terrible." Hrithik slumped on the bench. "Sameer won everything. He's a genius."
"I noticed something in your third game. You stopped and thought for a long time before moving your knight."
"I was trying to protect my queen."
"And did it work?"
"For a bit. Then I got scared and rushed."
"So you've found your next thing to practise: slowing down when you're scared. That's a real strategy."
Hrithik thought. "Can we play at home tonight? Slowly?"
"Slowly. And I'll probably lose."

qa.q: How many games did Hrithik lose?
qa.a: All five games.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling after the tournament?
qa.a: He felt terrible and defeated, comparing himself with Sameer.

qa.q: How did Parveen turn the loss into something useful?
qa.a: By noticing his careful thinking with the knight and naming a strategy to practise, instead of focusing on results.

qa.q: Why might Parveen say she will probably lose?
qa.a: She wants Hrithik to enjoy practising without pressure, showing that losing is ordinary and not a measure of worth.

grounding: Shows a parent praising strategy and effort after losses, so the child is willing to keep trying.

passage:
When I was in Class 4, I entered the inter-school drawing contest and didn't win anything. I cried the whole way home.
Papa didn't say, "Next time you'll win." He looked at my drawing for a long time. Then he said, "You tried shading the clouds with your finger. That was clever. And you gave your extra crayons to Meenu when hers broke. I saw that."
I said, "But I lost." He said, "You tried something new. I'm proud of that."
After that I stopped only drawing things I knew I could do well. I tried faces, which are hard. Now I'm in Class 6, and I entered the contest again, with a face. I didn't win this time either. But I wasn't scared to try it, and Papa still says "tell me how you did the eyes" first.
Rekha

qa.q: What did Rekha give Meenu at the contest?
qa.a: Extra crayons, when Meenu's broke.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on the way home from the first contest?
qa.a: Rekha felt sad and disappointed about losing, crying the whole way home.

qa.q: What did Papa praise, and how did it help Rekha?
qa.a: He praised trying finger-shading and giving crayons to Meenu, not the result, so Rekha stopped being scared of failing and started trying harder things like faces.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had only talked about winning next time?
qa.a: Rekha might have kept drawing only safe things, feeling worth depended on prizes, and been too scared to try faces.

grounding: Shows a father praising effort, strategy and kindness after a loss, so his child learns worth doesn't depend on winning and dares to try harder things.
